name: wazero
baseline: Wasmtime (cranelift); the same table also lists Wasmtime winch and Wasmer singlepass
workload: Time for each runtime to compile the benchmark guest module (pinky, prime-sieve, minimal) from the PolkaVM benchmark suite; wazero has no execution rows in that suite.
claimed_speedup: Compile time pinky: wazero 2.543 ms vs Wasmtime cranelift 62.212 ms (about 24x), Wasmtime winch 16.569 ms (about 6.5x) and Wasmer singlepass 3.946 ms (about 1.6x); prime-sieve: wazero 4.049 ms vs cranelift 76.662 ms (about 19x), winch 8.510 ms (about 2.1x), Wasmer singlepass 9.421 ms (about 2.3x); minimal: wazero 197.802 us vs cranelift 858.096 us (about 4.3x) and winch 575.089 us, but slower than Wasmer singlepass 85.955 us. All ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Harness is built with Rust 1.86.0, cargo --release, lto = true, codegen-units = 1 (benchtool); wazero is driven through a Go shared library loaded with libloading (feature 'wazero'); the page does not state the Go or wazero version
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3970X 32-Core, x86_64 Linux; results from commit 190ea5ac, timestamp 2024-11-24
stars_or_usage: 6.4k stars; pkg.go.dev shows 714 importers of github.com/tetratelabs/wazero v1.12.0
tradeoffs: Pure Go with zero dependencies and no CGO; compiler (amd64, arm64) and interpreter modes; no CGO means it embeds in Go programs without a C toolchain, but it is not callable from C++ directly.
caveats: Evidence is a third-party table (the PolkaVM author's suite), compile time only: wazero's execution speed against Wasmtime is not measured there, and its own README makes no baseline claim (it only says its Compiler is often 10x faster than its Interpreter); wazero version not stated on the page (November 2024 snapshot); Wasmer singlepass compiled the minimal module about 2.3x faster than wazero.
found_via: pkg.go.dev search 'webassembly' (wazero, 714 importers) and the compile-time tables in PolkaVM BENCHMARKS.md found through the crates.io search q='risc-v vm'

verification.tier_reason: The numbers are on BENCHMARKS.md, but the measurement is invalid. The benchtool Go shim (tools/benchtool/wazero/main.go at 190ea5ac, wazero v1.8.1) never calls CompiledModule.Close; Module_drop only removes a map entry. benchmark_compilation in tools/benchtool/src/main.rs calls compile count times on one runtime. wazero v1.8.1 runtime.CompileModule then hashes the binary into module.ID, and engine.CompileModule returns early on a compiledModules[module.ID] hit (internal/engine/wazevo/engine.go: 'cache hit!'). So every iteration after the first measures only decode + validate + sha256 + map lookup, while Wasmtime and Wasmer recompile each time.
verification.notes: Reject for invalid evidence. This follows the MQF no-op precedent: the timed loop skips the work it claims to measure. I traced it through the shim's main.go (no Close), benchtool's benchmark_compilation (count compiles per engine) and the cache-hit early return in wazero v1.8.1 engine.CompileModule. If the orchestrator keeps wazero, it should be as an incumbent baseline with no faster-than claim. The metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 6.4k stars, last commit 2026-09-28. The canonical repo is now wazero/wazero.
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence (MQF precedent): the only baseline claim is the PolkaVM benchtool compile-time row, but the benchtool's wazero shim never calls CompiledModule.Close and wazero v1.8.1 engine.CompileModule returns early on an in-memory module-ID cache hit, so the compile rows time decode, validate and hash rather than compilation. No other baseline comparison exists. Repo now at wazero/wazero.

name: Pipa (pipa-js)
workload: V8 benchmark suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes) run by the pipa, QuickJS (qjs), Node and Boa binaries, dated 2026-06-15 in the README.
claimed_speedup: README says 'outperforms QuickJS in benchmarks', but its own table shows total score 1075 vs qjs 1101 (-2.4%). Faster than qjs on RegExp (841 vs 306, +174.8%) and NavierStokes (2087 vs 1759, +18.6%); slower on RayTrace (589 vs 1268), EarleyBoyer (1225 vs 1831), Splay (2000 vs 2206), Richards, DeltaBlue and Crypto.
tradeoffs: Pure Rust register VM, about 5.2 MB binary, no C dependencies, embeddable as the pipa-js crate. Partial ES2023: README test262 table shows Proxy 0%, Promise 5.6%, Set 18.8%, Map 22.2%, RegExp 42.3%.
caveats: Headline claim contradicts the README's own overall score (slightly slower than QuickJS); the win is confined to RegExp and NavierStokes. No CPU, flags or QuickJS version stated. A search snippet of an earlier announcement quoted 1256 vs 1219 (not on the page opened, so not used). Added mainly as a regex-engine data point; low conformance weakens the RegExp comparison.
found_via: WebSearch 'new JavaScript engine written in Rust OR Zig OR Go ... beating QuickJS' -> dev.to post (blocked) -> restsend/pipa

verification.tier_reason: The README table (2026-06-15) comes from the public bench-v8.sh (runs boa-dev's combined.js V8 suite once per engine) with release flags in Cargo.toml, but no CPU model, rustc version or qjs version/build is stated; first-party, so C.
verification.notes: Numbers match the README table exactly; record already reports that pipa is slower than qjs overall. Main shortcomings: not faster overall (score -2.4%), single-run harness, unknown qjs build, low test262 conformance behind the RegExp win, no LICENSE file (MIT only in Cargo.toml/README).
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence (stb-zip precedent): the only clear win, the V8 RegExp suite (841 vs qjs 306), comes from a fast path that does not run a regular expression: string_replace with a RegExp does a literal s.find on the pattern source (same code at 4a4dfd0 of 2026-06-14 and at HEAD), regexp_exec returns no capture groups, String.match is literal too, and the 712 replace calls in the suite all take a regex; the suite checks no results and the harness reports 'ok' despite errors. Without the RegExp row Pipa scores 1114 against qjs 1321, about 16% slower, so no valid win remains.

name: R8 (NoClip, Rust V8)
workload: 12 workloads from the js-engines-benchmark suite (arithmetic loops, recursion, object operations, memory, arrays, strings, cryptography, algorithms, WebSockets, databases, HTTP routing, package resolution).
claimed_speedup: js-engines-benchmark README (https://github.com/NoClip/js-engines-benchmark): R8 '3.08x faster overall' than Google V8 TurboFan across 12 benchmarks (suite total 19.43 ms vs 59.82 ms), individual speedups from 1.38x (arithmetic) to 11.13x (HTTP routing).
tradeoffs: Described as a pure-Rust engine 'based on Google V8 version 12.8'; no C++ API; extremely young (first visible commit 2026-09-14, about 20-27 commits).
caveats: Very low confidence. Same author runs the engine and the benchmark repo; hardware, date and flags are not stated; each workload takes only a few milliseconds; the benchmark repo has a commit about preserving upstream function names and verifying honest execution 'without R8 cheats', which suggests harness-gaming concerns; the r8 README table (arithmetic loops 4.13 ms vs V8 7.82 ms) does not match the 1.38x figure on the benchmark repo page. A from-scratch Rust reimplementation of V8 that beats V8 TurboFan 3x in a month is not credible without independent reproduction. Included so the verifier can check the harness; expect rejection if the benchmark is invalid.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'JavaScript engine faster than V8 benchmark github open source JIT Octane Speedometer results' surfaced NoClip/js-engines-benchmark

verification.tier_reason: The numbers exist on the js-engines-benchmark README, but R8's interpreter (src/interpreter/interpreter.rs, added in commit 1c1b5cf 'achieve 100% benchmark domination over V8 and Bun across all 12 workloads') special-cases the suite: FusedPackageResolverLoop fires only when the loop body is 121 bytes and calls a global named 'resolveDependencies', then skips the resolver and adds a hard-coded pass_hash of 34354737 per iteration; FusedExpressPipelineLoop (body 87 bytes, global 'parseHttpRequest') never parses HTTP and computes the checksum from a closed-form length formula; similar name-keyed paths exist for 'readRowHash' and 'unmaskFrame', and FusedCryptoCallLoop swaps the benchmark's 72-byte myHash function for a native Rust copy with the seed 21661362 baked in. The timed work is not executed, so the evidence is invalid.
verification.notes: Reject for invalid evidence (MQF and zokio precedents): R8 pattern-matches the benchmark suite's function names and loop byte lengths and returns hard-coded or closed-form checksums instead of executing the timed JavaScript, and the published table also predates the removal of a 1 ms timer clamp. Metadata checked: MIT, 2 stars, 0 forks, 20 commits, last commit 2026-09-19; harness repo MIT, 1 star, 27 commits, last commit 2026-09-19.
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence (MQF and zokio precedent): src/interpreter/interpreter.rs (commit 1c1b5cf) pattern-matches the benchmark suite's function names and loop byte lengths (readRowHash, unmaskFrame, parseHttpRequest, resolveDependencies) and replaces them with fused native loops that skip the work: FusedPackageResolverLoop skips the resolver and returns a hard-coded pass_hash 34354737, FusedExpressPipelineLoop computes the checksum in closed form without parsing HTTP, FusedCryptoCallLoop swaps myHash for native Rust. The README table also predates the fix of a Math.max(1, ...) timer clamp (seven R8 cells read 1.00 ms).
